recent_posts.author: it44
recent_posts.content_text:
Good scope: testing the transaction shape, not only the happy path. Your first phase leaves the since usage and serialization open, so here are five CKB-specific decisions I would settle in the week-1 spec, because each one changes what the tests have to check. I read the proposal and the CKB RFCs, then ran points 1 and 4 on a local CKB dev chain (ckb 0.210.0), and points 3 and 5 and the group case on a deliberately simple toy lock script of mine in ckb-testtool (so “naive” below means my toy, not your design). Point 2 is a design decision and was not run. Happy to share the scripts.
Relative timeouts restart on every milestone. A relative since is measured from the block that committed the transaction that created the input cell. If each release re-creates the escrow cell with the remainder, the refund clock restarts every time. On the dev chain, a relative since of 15 blocks was rejected right after creation (Immature), accepted after 15 blocks, and the re-created cell was rejected again right away with the same since. An absolute deadline did not restart: the re-created cell was spendable immediately after the deadline. Decide between an absolute deadline and restart-on-purpose, and test both.
After the timeout, is release still valid? Both paths spend the same cell, so after the deadline a refund and a late release are competing transactions, and ordering decides the outcome, not the contract’s intent. If release stays valid, a refund can be front-run by a late release, and the other way round. Pick one rule and test the race.
Fees on permissionless paths. Fee is inputs minus outputs and goes to the miner. On an authorized path the sender only burns their own funds, but if anyone can trigger the refund after the timeout, a transaction with outputs below the escrowed capacity lets a third party burn it (the difference goes to the miner). In my toy lock, a refund paying 400 of 1000 was accepted by the naive check and rejected once the lock required outputs of at least the escrowed capacity. Require that, and fees from another input.
Minimum capacity breaks small milestones. Every output must hold at least its occupied capacity (61 CKB for a plain secp256k1 lock cell with no data; yours will differ with args and data). On the dev chain a 60.99999999 CKB output was rejected (InsufficientCellCapacity), 61 was accepted, and a 1000 CKB cell could not be split 950/50 or 970/30 because the remainder cell was below the minimum. Any milestone that would leave a remainder below that minimum cannot be released, so the funds sit until the refund path. Worth a fixture, and a note in the docs.
Terms are not checked at creation. A lock only runs when its cell is spent, so anyone can create a cell with your lock args and any terms, for example a timeout of zero. In my toy test a cell with the escrow lock, deadline 0 and “approved” state was created from an unrelated cell’s input and accepted. To the seller it looks like a real escrow. A type script (with a unique id) can enforce well-formed terms at creation; either way the docs should say that the counterparty must check the args against what was agreed.
On the group case in “transaction isolation”: a lock group contains only input cells and runs once per transaction, so release logic must count its group inputs and bind exactly one continuation output through Source::Output. With two escrow cells in one transaction where only one was approved, the naive lock (which looked at the first cell only) accepted it and the hardened lock rejected it.
One suggestion on acceptance: make the independent reproduction a milestone gate, not “subject to reviewer availability”.
Sources: RFC 0017 (tx valid since), RFC 0022 (transaction structure).

recent_posts.author: psawyerberlin
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @devnash, this is a really useful kit. Timeout and refund paths are exactly where escrow scripts tend to break.
I’m the author of CSR (CKB Service Runner), and there’s one application-level gap I’d suggest documenting: the script can permit a refund once the timeout has passed, but someone still has to submit that refund transaction. Today that’s usually the user or the project’s own server.
With CSR, the escrow creator (or the app) posts a job cell with an at block or at time trigger that matches the refund timeout. The runner proves the trigger through the since field, reads the escrow cell through a chain-read host call, and returns the refund transaction skeleton to the refund recipient committed in the lock args. A “when cell X is spent” condition can cancel the job if the escrow is released first.
That could also make a nice extra test case: refund liveness with no trusted server.
Status, honestly: CSR’s runtime and contracts are testnet only, and mainnet paid services are gated until the runner set is large and diverse enough. An October audit found no critical issues, and fixes are underway. If you’d like a testnet job pointed at your reference escrow, I’m glad to help.

recent_posts.topic_title: Noir-CKB: the private tally is live on CKB testnet, try it yourself
recent_posts.author: xiaomao
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi Patrick,
I didn’t know VoteSecure existed, and it’s really cool to find someone who’s been working on private voting on CKB this long. I’m going to read the v2.3 spec properly this week.
Dropping drand for threshold decryption is the right call, I think. I hadn’t thought about the problem where the person generating the key could just look before the release round, and once you see it, you can’t really unsee it. Same with the live totals. Decrypting a running sum twice and getting the votes in between is the kind of leak I would have walked straight into.
I did notice something about the batching that might bite you though. One Groth16 verification costs about 117M cycles in my tests, and a CKB block can only use 3.5B cycles in total, so you can fit fewer than 30 proof verifications in a block. If the relay puts lots of ballots into one Ballot Box transaction and each ballot has its own proof, you’ll hit that limit pretty quickly. On the other hand, Groth16 verification doesn’t really get more expensive as the circuit gets bigger, so a membership proof over a deep Merkle tree would cost about the same to verify as my tally proof does.
I was also wondering where you want the 0-or-1 validity proofs to live. If they’re inside a SNARK, the circuit has to do elliptic curve operations over the ElGamal ciphertexts, and that gets expensive fast. Are you planning to do them in Noir, or as sigma proofs that the script checks directly? I feel like that one choice decides a lot of your cycle budget.
The anonymous membership and nullifier part is where I think we could actually build something together. A Noir circuit that proves you’re in the voter tree and gives a nullifier per election, taken through noir-ckb so the proof is bound to the Ballot Box transition, with real cycle numbers. It’s small enough to actually finish, it would close your biggest privacy gap, and it would be the first time noir-ckb gets used for something that isn’t my own example.
I’m also writing the relayer test this week, where a different account pays the fee and any change to the tally gets rejected. Once it works I’d love to compare it with your escrow design.

recent_posts.content_text:
gm!
I’m one of the ceremony contributors, and I came back to this as a reader working through the step-by-step guide on Ubuntu 24.04. Taking your first question first, because I did get stuck.
The two-command path works. The step-by-step guide does not, if you have no nargo of your own:
$ python3 -B scripts/start-counter.py doctor
OK: Nargo beta.18 and compiler pin
Prerequisite checks passed.
$ python3 -B scripts/setup-private-tally.py --out target/my-tally-setup \
--backend ../Noir-Groth16 --ptau target/ppot_0080_12.ptau \
--ceremony ceremony/private-tally-v2
RuntimeError: Nargo 1.0.0-beta.18 (99bb8b5c) required
The doctor probes nargo through tool_environment(), which puts the pinned tools first on PATH. setup-private-tally.py defaults --nargo to the bare string, so it gets whatever PATH already had. try-private-tally.py goes through tool_environment() as well, which is why the two commands in your post are fine and only the guide’s longer path breaks.
What made it slow to find: the troubleshooting table sends an R1CS mismatch to “run the doctor again”, and the doctor passes. So the suggested remedy can’t diagnose it. With no nargo at all it’s a bare FileNotFoundError.
Fix on my side, in case someone else lands here:
export PATH="$PWD/target/counter-tools/linux-x86_64:$PATH"
Then your second question, what I’d build with it.
A commitment scheme has two halves, committing and opening, and the Cell has the committing half. Right now the only way to open it is to hand over (value, r, key), which gives away the exact number. So: a circuit that proves a bound on the hidden value instead, checked against the commitment that is already on chain.
github.com/wamimi/noir-ckb-verifier
feat: range proof over a private tally commitment (#8)
main ← CECILIA-MULANDI:circuits/private-tally-range
opened 01:03AM - 09 Nov 26 UTC
CECILIA-MULANDI
+137
-0
## What this adds
`circuits/private-tally-range/`, a Noir circuit proving a com…mitted tally's hidden value lies within a range, without revealing it.
```text
public: c, lo, hi
private: value, blinding, key
```
It reuses `circuits/private-tally-v2/commitment` unchanged, so a proof here opens exactly the commitment the deployed Type Script stores. One circuit covers four shapes: `lo = 3, hi = 9` for a range, `hi = 2^64 - 1` for at least, `lo = 0` for at most, and `lo = hi` for an exact value.
## Why
A commitment scheme has two halves, committing and opening. The tally has the committing half. Today the owner cannot prove anything about the value to anyone: disclosing `(value, r, key)` hands over the exact number, and an observer can only infer a weak bound from the update count, since each `delta` is constrained to 32 bits. This adds the opening half, done selectively, so a claim like "the tally is at least 1000" can be checked against the commitment already on chain without the opening.
Worth being straight about where this came from: nobody asked for it. It is not on your list of what voting still needs, and it is not the membership and nullifier gap from the forum thread. It is the primitive that usually accompanies a hiding commitment, offered in case it is useful rather than presented as a gap you left.
## What it does not do
It authorizes nothing. There is no transaction binding, so a proof here is a reusable bearer attestation, never permission to update a Cell. A verifier has to check two things the circuit cannot: that `c` is the commitment the Cell holds now, since every update rerandomizes, and that `(lo, hi)` is the range it asked about. Both are stated in a comment at the top of `src/main.nr`.
## Checks
Nargo 1.0.0-beta.18 (`99bb8b5c`), `noir-lang/poseidon` v0.2.6 (`00f87918`), backend `828025f3`, snarkjs 0.7.5.
| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `nargo test` | 18 passed (6 accepting, 12 rejecting) |
| `nargo fmt --check` | Clean |
| R1CS size | 1,749 constraints, 1,750 wires; 3 private, 3 public inputs, 0 outputs |
| `snarkjs wtns check` | `WITNESS IS CORRECT` |
| Visibility | Public values in wires 1–3 in order; leak scan clean |
| Phase 1 reuse | Fits the power-12 ceiling of 4,096, so `ppot_0080_12.ptau` is reusable |
`private-tally-v2` is 3,338 constraints for comparison.
## Setup
Phase 2 is circuit specific, so proving with this needs its own key. A single-party development key is enough to exercise the circuit, so nothing here asks you for a ceremony. If this ever gets a real user, that is when a multi-party phase 2 would be worth your time.
Useful either way: a phase 2 key is bound to one R1CS, and `ceremony-private-tally.py` freezes `r1cs_sha256` when a ceremony opens. So if you want anything changed about the constraints, before a key exists is the cheap time to say so.
The package is deliberately outside the `private-tally-v2` workspace, so `nargo compile --workspace` keeps producing the artifact the ceremony froze.
One circuit covers a range, at-least, at-most and exact-value. It reuses the private-tally-v2 commitment unchanged, so a proof opens exactly what the deployed Type Script stores, and at 1,749 constraints against v2’s 3,338 it still fits under the power-12 ceiling, so ppot_0080_12.ptau is reusable. It authorizes nothing, to be clear: there is no transaction binding, so a proof is a reusable bearer attestation and never permission to update a Cell.
If that PATH default is worth fixing in the scripts rather than in my shell, say so and I will send it separately.

recent_posts.content_text:
GM xiaomao, Cecilia,
I ran the private tally today on Ubuntu 24.04 under WSL2 (x86_64), repo at commit b481cfc.
Your question 1: did it work? Yes, first time. Install took under 3 minutes, the first run about 17 (10 of those were me typing passwords). One creation and five hidden additions, all committed on testnet:
creation: 0x9a6ba035…3fb3, 114.6M cycles
updates: 0xb9634f37…2d04, 0x44001cfa…ecbc, 0x9bbe022d…8229, 0x4dba4459…c9ff, 0xdae0d5cd…d546, about 117M cycles each
The amounts were 112, 1112, 10112, the maximum 4294967295, and then 0 as a cover update. The final total, 4294978631, was correct and went past 2^32, so the 32-bit limit is per addition, as the guide says. The cover update left the value unchanged, and on chain it has the same size and shape as the others. Typing 4294967296 was refused at the prompt, with nothing sent.
Local test suite on x86_64: start-counter.py tally-local passed all 10 stages, including the 49-case CKB-VM matrix and the 4 mutation tests. The doctor still notes that the matrix has not run on x86_64, so this may be the first run there. The unit tests pass too (74/74 with the pinned nargo).
The guide’s longer path: Cecilia, I can confirm your report on x86_64, in the “no nargo at all” form: the doctor passes, then setup-private-tally.py stops with FileNotFoundError: 'nargo'. Your PATH workaround fixes it. One more thing to know: the failed run leaves target/my-tally-setup/ behind, so rerunning the same command fails with FileExistsError until you delete that folder. After that, the setup passed, and its verification key hash matched the ceremony’s. I’ll send xiaomao the details separately.
On your voting points, xiaomao: the 0-or-1 validity proofs are planned as sigma proofs (disjunctive Chaum-Pedersen) checked directly by the script, not inside a SNARK. So the Noir circuit would only carry membership and the nullifier, at a fixed ~117M cycles, and the ElGamal curve can stay secp256k1. Your cycle point is taken: under 30 Groth16 checks per block caps the relay batch size, and I’ll put that into the spec.
And yes to building the membership + nullifier circuit together. As a first step, within the next two weeks I’ll write down VoteSecure’s requirements for that circuit: what the proof must show, exactly what it has to be bound to on a Ballot Box transition, and what it must leave open, such as the fee inputs, so that any relayer can pay without being able to change the ballot. That gives you a fixed target to build against in noir-ckb. The requirements will live at `docs/specs/ballot-membership-binding.md’ in the VoteSecure repo, with a GitHub issue for comments.

recent_posts.author: ebubedev
recent_posts.content_text:
Here is what changed since 7902998 through 8969e95
1. Keep the fiat-sent report when the route drops after the bank transfer
Removed the old refuse_fiat_if_route_blocked path that rejected fiat-sent before recording anything.
fiat-sent now records first (fiat_sent_at + fiat-sent-ok), then checks the route separately via route_after_fiat_sent.
If the dry-run path is gone, the trade moves to awaiting-invoice without clearing fiat_sent_at, and both sides get a new-invoice notice. The buyer can send the same payment hash again; the seller can still release while that recovery is in progress.
Pre-fiat failures still stay in awaiting-route / need-route and still refuse fiat-sent until a route exists (so the buyer is not told to pay bank-side before the wallet can receive).
Added fiat_opened (set when fiat instructions are offered / waiting-fiat). A dispute cannot start the release clock via fiat-sent until that window was actually opened.
2. Deadlines follow the real inbound claim delay and the buyer invoice lock
inbound_hold now returns both the earliest live inbound TLC expiry and the channel’s tlc_expiry_delta. Claim margin is channel_delta + CHECK_CHANNELS_INTERVAL, floored at Fiber’s default (160m + 60s), and persisted per trade as claim_margin_ms.
The buyer invoice’s final_htlc_minimum_expiry_delta is stored as final_tlc_expiry_delta_ms (defaulting to Fiber’s 24h when omitted) and fed into pay_by, route_by, invoice “must last” checks, and the outgoing tlc_expiry_limit budget.
Published windows no longer assume a fixed claim margin plus Fiber’s shortest invoice lock: a slower inbound channel or a longer final delta shortens usable fiat/payout time the same way Fiber will.
Hold invoices moved from 36h → 48h so the default final TLC plus the 2h release grace and 4h solver window still fit.
Other changes in that range
If a payout already succeeded (or a preimage is known) while Fiber reports the hold as Expired, the daemon prefers local settle over expiring the trade.
twine-push NIP-98 auth and TWINE_PUSH_PUBLIC_URL for reverse-proxy setups.

3. Project Description
Problem
With initiatives like NNCBN (Nervos Network Community Boot Nodes) proving the importance of network operator diversity, expanding the count of community-hosted L1 nodes and Layer 2 Fiber Network Nodes (fnn) is critical to decentralizing state and liquidity.
However, setting up a light-client node alongside a Fiber payment node on low-cost hardware (e.g., Raspberry Pi 4/5, RockPi, or cheap ARM/x86 VPS) presents significant friction for non-enterprise operators:
Manually building/downloading ckb-light-client and fnn binaries for specific architectures (ARM64 vs. x86_64).
Writing systemd unit files to manage background service lifecycles, auto-restarts, and log rotation manually.
Risk of Channel Data Loss: Unlike L1 nodes, a Fiber Network Node (fnn) maintains stateful off-chain payment channels. If an unmanaged home device suffers a power outage or crash without automated, event-triggered channel store backups, the operator risks losing funds and channel data.
Solution
CKB-Up a ckb-fiber-node-installer provides an open-source, automated 1-click installation script (curl -sSL https://…/install.sh | bash) designed specifically for headless Linux systems (Ubuntu/Debian/Raspbian).
It automates binary retrieval, daemon generation, network port configuration, and installs a lightweight background service (fnn-backup-daemon) that safely creates encrypted snapshots of the local Fiber channel database whenever channel state updates.

Auto-detects Linux distribution, architecture (aarch64 / x86_64), and available storage.

Downloads verified release binaries for both ckb-light-client and fnn.
systemd Management & Environment Templates:
Automated creation and enabling of system services (ckb-light-client.service and fnn.service).

A lightweight background utility that watches the fnn store directory (/fiber/store).

The problem
When you buy a used phone or laptop, you rely on what the seller tells you about repairs. Repair shops here mostly don’t keep records either, they rely on what the owner says.

Each device gets a passport, a cell on CKB with its history in the cell data

recent_posts.author: SalmanDev
recent_posts.content_text:
Tranfr: Project Completion Report
Programmable recovery for CKB self-custody
Report date: 9 November 2026 | Applicant: SalmanDev | Status: testnet deployment
1. Summary
Tranfr is a CKB lock script, a TypeScript SDK and a testnet web demo that give a self-custodied cell a recovery path. The owner keeps full control at all times. A designated recovery recipient can claim the cell only after an on-chain deadline has passed. The owner extends the deadline by renewing the cell, an ordinary owner spend that recreates it with a later deadline. Nothing depends on a custodian, oracle or off-chain service.
The design follows the program reviewer’s feedback on the original proposal: the hard-freeze model and the custom state machine were dropped, the owner can always spend, the recipient can claim once the deadline is reached, the heartbeat is an off-chain agreement with a 90-day default set in the frontend, and the SDK and frontend are treated as first-class deliverables.
Following that feedback, the Time Lock + Cheque composition was built and tested. It cannot pay native CKB to a recipient, so the delivered lock is a single purpose-built script that implements the same rules. This is documented with a runnable test suite (section 5).
The reviewer also raised a capacity concern for typed cells such as UDTs. The lock now includes a typed-cell refund rule (section 3).
image371×846 14.4 KB
image373×846 16.4 KB
2. Scope and design decisions
Requirement from feedback
Outcome
No hard freeze, no custom state machine
Done. There are two unlock paths and no stored state transitions.
Owner can always take the assets, even after the deadline
Done. The owner path is unconditional.
Recipient can take the assets once the deadline is reached
Done. The recipient path is gated by an absolute epoch since on every input in the script group.
Heartbeat is off-chain, 90 days by default, longer allowed
Done. Renewal is an owner spend that recreates the cell with a later deadline. The default is 540 epochs (about 90 days) and any longer period is allowed.
SDK and frontend are first-class
Done. A standalone TypeScript SDK and a web demo are in the repo.
Combine Time Lock with Cheque
Evaluated and not viable for native CKB. See section 5.
Capacity concern for typed assets
Addressed with a type-script branch in the recipient path. See section 3.
3. What was built
3.1 Tranfr lock script
Owner path. Valid at any time, before or after the deadline. Authorized by the owner’s signature.
Recipient path. Valid only when every input in the script group carries an absolute epoch since at or after the deadline stored in the cell’s args, and the recipient has signed.
Typed-cell refund rule. On a recipient claim, the capacity of any input that carries a type script (for example a UDT cell) must be returned to the owner, meaning the owner-locked outputs must total at least that capacity. Plain CKB cells carry no type script and the recipient takes them in full. Mixed transactions only need to refund the typed part. Sums use u128 so many capacities cannot overflow.
Args layout. Fixed width, 72 bytes, with full-length hashes. The minimum capacity of a Tranfr cell is therefore 113 CKB. Full-length hashes were kept for the larger collision margin.
Deployment. The testnet deployment is described in docs/deployment.md. It uses a Type ID, so the deployer can upgrade the binary.
What the lock does not do: it does not check the token output of a typed claim (amount, type or destination). Delivering the tokens to the recipient is the transaction builder’s job. The lock enforces only the owner’s capacity refund.
3.2 TypeScript SDK
A standalone package that builds to sdk/dist, with no imports outside its own directory. It covers creating a Tranfr, inspecting its policy and status, renewing, owner reclaim, and recipient claim.
Owner and recipient locks are validated as standard secp256k1 sighash locks, so funds cannot be locked behind an unusable lock type.
Renewal keeps the cell’s own inactivity period, with a minimum of 90 days, and refuses an earlier deadline unless the caller allows it explicitly. A heartbeat therefore cannot silently shorten a longer period.
Builders preserve type scripts on typed cells and require the type script’s cell deps. For typed claims, buildRecoveryClaim adds the owner refund output.
3.3 Web demo
A web application for the full lifecycle: create, renew, claim, reclaim, with the cell’s state and transaction status shown at each stage. It was redesigned in the final phase and is exercised by Playwright end-to-end specs.
Wallet view: Tranfr — recovery policy (CKB Testnet)
The standalone version is still https://tranfr-jet.vercel.app if you want to see the full flow including the recipient claim.
3.4 Documentation
The repo contains docs/spec.md, docs/security-model.md, docs/deployment.md, docs/implementation-plan.md, docs/testnet-evidence.md, docs/composition-evaluation.md and docs/cargo-test-output.txt. The README describes the delivered design.
4. Verification
4.1 Automated tests
Rust: 56 tests, all passing (saved output in docs/cargo-test-output.txt): 11 since-comparison tests, 34 integration tests (26 lock tests plus 8 composition tests) and 11 lock unit tests.
Lock coverage: both unlock paths, deadline boundaries, relative and other since metrics, every-input-in-group checks, the mode byte, malformed args and witnesses, signature tampering, and replay. New refund-rule cases: typed claim with no refund fails, typed claim with an underpaid refund fails, typed claim with a full refund passes, plain claim is unchanged, and mixed inputs refund only the typed part.
TypeScript: 47 SDK tests, all passing. Typecheck and build are clean.
4.2 Testnet lifecycle
The full run is recorded with explorer links in docs/testnet-evidence.md. Highlights:
Plain cells. Create, extend (owner renew), owner reclaim before the deadline, recipient claim after the deadline (199.99999236 CKB paid to the recipient, transaction 0x024f847f…1c35), and owner reclaim after the deadline (199.99999644 CKB paid to the owner, transaction 0x1f405df1…2ee8).
Early claim rejected. The SDK refuses to build an early claim. With the SDK check bypassed, the node itself rejects it as immature because of the since requirement.
Typed cell (UDT). A 200 CKB cell carrying 1,000,000 xUDT was claimed by the recipient after the deadline (transaction 0x5d0ae5b6…4343). The cell’s 200 CKB capacity was refunded to the owner as a plain cell, and the xUDT went to the recipient’s own token cell.
5. Time Lock + Cheque evaluation
The suggested composition was tested under ckb-testtool using the vendored testnet binaries, whose data hashes are asserted in the tests. Both role assignments were tried.
The recipient’s claim cannot pay the recipient. With the recipient on the Cheque receiver path, RFC 0039 rule 1.b.ii requires the Cheque’s capacity to be returned to the sender. Paying the recipient fails with Cheque error 8 (SenderCapacityNotSame).
Swapping the roles blocks the owner. The same rule then forces the owner’s own reclaim to send the capacity to the sender, so the owner cannot take their funds back as plain CKB.
The owner is locked out for six epochs after every spend. The Cheque sender path accepts only a relative since of six epochs (about 24 hours), so each create or renew would freeze the owner for a day. Before the window it fails with Cheque error 11.
No role assignment delivers both “the recipient claims the CKB after the deadline” and “the owner can reclaim the CKB at any time.” Cheque is built for token transfers, where returning the capacity to the sender is the right behavior. The Tranfr lock keeps that behavior only where it is wanted, for typed cells.
The tests are in tests/src/composition.rs. A correction was also made during this work: an earlier draft of docs/implementation-plan.md wrongly said the Time Lock does not exist. It does, under ckb-devrel/ckb-proxy-locks, and it is listed on docs.nervos.org with mainnet and testnet deployments. The plan is corrected and the evaluation document records this.
6. Security model and known limitations
Unaudited, testnet only. No production audit has been done. Do not use this with real funds.
Owner race after the deadline. Because the owner path never freezes, the owner and recipient can race after the deadline. This is intended and documented in the security model.
Typed assets. The lock enforces only the capacity refund. Preserving the tokens in the recipient’s output is the builder’s responsibility, and typed cells need the type script’s cell deps.
Standard lock types only. Owner and recipient must use the standard secp256k1 sighash lock. The SDK rejects anything else.
Upgradeable deployment. The testnet deployment uses a Type ID, so the deployer controls the binary.
Minimum capacity. 113 CKB per cell. Shrinking the args to 20-byte hashes would lower this to 89 CKB but was not done, and would require redeploying and repeating the testnet evidence.
Testnet test conditions. The recorded lifecycles used short deadlines (one epoch), not the 540-epoch default, and the demo was driven with an injected test wallet, not a production wallet such as JoyID or MetaMask.
Out of scope: multiple recipients, social or threshold recovery, notifications, production wallet integration, Fiber channel funds, and a security audit.
7. How to verify
Run the Rust tests: cargo test and the composition suite with cargo test --manifest-path tests/Cargo.toml composition.
Run the SDK checks: npm ci, then npx tsc --noEmit, npx tsc -p tsconfig.build.json and npx tsx --test sdk/tests/*.test.ts.
Open the transaction links in docs/testnet-evidence.md and compare each against its description.
Read docs/spec.md and docs/security-model.md against contracts/tranfr-lock/.
8. Next steps
A third-party security audit before any mainnet use.
Decide whether to shrink the args to 20-byte hashes to lower the minimum capacity.
Run the full 540-epoch lifecycle on testnet and test with production wallets.
Integration examples for wallets and apps, including node-side runners that could host the lock.
A proposal for further funding, covering the audit, wallet integration and mainnet deployment.

3.3 Web demo

A web application for the full lifecycle: create, renew, claim, reclaim, with the cell’s state and transaction status shown at each stage. It was redesigned in the final phase and is exercised by Playwright end-to-end specs.

Wallet view: Tranfr — recovery policy (CKB Testnet)

The standalone version is still https://tranfr-jet.vercel.app if you want to see the full flow including the recipient claim.

3.4 Documentation

The repo contains docs/spec.md, docs/security-model.md, docs/deployment.md, docs/implementation-plan.md, docs/testnet-evidence.md, docs/composition-evaluation.md and docs/cargo-test-output.txt. The README describes the delivered design.

4. Verification

4.1 Automated tests

  • Rust: 56 tests, all passing (saved output in docs/cargo-test-output.txt): 11 since-comparison tests, 34 integration tests (26 lock tests plus 8 composition tests) and 11 lock unit tests.

  • Lock coverage: both unlock paths, deadline boundaries, relative and other since metrics, every-input-in-group checks, the mode byte, malformed args and witnesses, signature tampering, and replay. New refund-rule cases: typed claim with no refund fails, typed claim with an underpaid refund fails, typed claim with a full refund passes, plain claim is unchanged, and mixed inputs refund only the typed part.

  • TypeScript: 47 SDK tests, all passing. Typecheck and build are clean.

4.2 Testnet lifecycle

The full run is recorded with explorer links in docs/testnet-evidence.md. Highlights:

  • Plain cells. Create, extend (owner renew), owner reclaim before the deadline, recipient claim after the deadline (199.99999236 CKB paid to the recipient, transaction 0x024f847f…1c35), and owner reclaim after the deadline (199.99999644 CKB paid to the owner, transaction 0x1f405df1…2ee8).

  • Early claim rejected. The SDK refuses to build an early claim. With the SDK check bypassed, the node itself rejects it as immature because of the since requirement.

  • Typed cell (UDT). A 200 CKB cell carrying 1,000,000 xUDT was claimed by the recipient after the deadline (transaction 0x5d0ae5b6…4343). The cell’s 200 CKB capacity was refunded to the owner as a plain cell, and the xUDT went to the recipient’s own token cell.

5. Time Lock + Cheque evaluation

The suggested composition was tested under ckb-testtool using the vendored testnet binaries, whose data hashes are asserted in the tests. Both role assignments were tried.

  1. The recipient’s claim cannot pay the recipient. With the recipient on the Cheque receiver path, RFC 0039 rule 1.b.ii requires the Cheque’s capacity to be returned to the sender. Paying the recipient fails with Cheque error 8 (SenderCapacityNotSame).

  2. Swapping the roles blocks the owner. The same rule then forces the owner’s own reclaim to send the capacity to the sender, so the owner cannot take their funds back as plain CKB.

  3. The owner is locked out for six epochs after every spend. The Cheque sender path accepts only a relative since of six epochs (about 24 hours), so each create or renew would freeze the owner for a day. Before the window it fails with Cheque error 11.

No role assignment delivers both “the recipient claims the CKB after the deadline” and “the owner can reclaim the CKB at any time.” Cheque is built for token transfers, where returning the capacity to the sender is the right behavior. The Tranfr lock keeps that behavior only where it is wanted, for typed cells.

The tests are in tests/src/composition.rs. A correction was also made during this work: an earlier draft of docs/implementation-plan.md wrongly said the Time Lock does not exist. It does, under ckb-devrel/ckb-proxy-locks, and it is listed on docs.nervos.org with mainnet and testnet deployments. The plan is corrected and the evaluation document records this.

6. Security model and known limitations

  • Unaudited, testnet only. No production audit has been done. Do not use this with real funds.

  • Owner race after the deadline. Because the owner path never freezes, the owner and recipient can race after the deadline. This is intended and documented in the security model.

  • Typed assets. The lock enforces only the capacity refund. Preserving the tokens in the recipient’s output is the builder’s responsibility, and typed cells need the type script’s cell deps.

  • Standard lock types only. Owner and recipient must use the standard secp256k1 sighash lock. The SDK rejects anything else.

  • Upgradeable deployment. The testnet deployment uses a Type ID, so the deployer controls the binary.

  • Minimum capacity. 113 CKB per cell. Shrinking the args to 20-byte hashes would lower this to 89 CKB but was not done, and would require redeploying and repeating the testnet evidence.

  • Testnet test conditions. The recorded lifecycles used short deadlines (one epoch), not the 540-epoch default, and the demo was driven with an injected test wallet, not a production wallet such as JoyID or MetaMask.

  • Out of scope: multiple recipients, social or threshold recovery, notifications, production wallet integration, Fiber channel funds, and a security audit.

7. How to verify

  1. Run the Rust tests: cargo test and the composition suite with cargo test --manifest-path tests/Cargo.toml composition.

  2. Run the SDK checks: npm ci, then npx tsc --noEmit, npx tsc -p tsconfig.build.json and npx tsx --test sdk/tests/*.test.ts.

  3. Open the transaction links in docs/testnet-evidence.md and compare each against its description.

  4. Read docs/spec.md and docs/security-model.md against contracts/tranfr-lock/.

8. Next steps

  • A third-party security audit before any mainnet use.

  • Decide whether to shrink the args to 20-byte hashes to lower the minimum capacity.

  • Run the full 540-epoch lifecycle on testnet and test with production wallets.

  • Integration examples for wallets and apps, including node-side runners that could host the lock.

  • A proposal for further funding, covering the audit, wallet integration and mainnet deployment.

recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_text:
image1920×1080 357 KB
On CKB a lock is a program, so “prove this wallet is mine” has no single answer. A secp256k1 key, a JoyID passkey, a multisig, Omnilock in one of its modes and a smart-account lock each prove control a different way, and a site that wants to check one has to write code for each.
Ward gives them one answer. The wallet signs a transaction that can never be committed. The verifier rebuilds that transaction itself, reads the lock’s cell deps from the chain, and runs the lock in CKB-VM. Exit 0 means the wallet controls the lock. One verifier handles every lock that signs the transaction hash, and any wallet that can sign an ordinary transaction can sign the proof, with no new code on either side. It is the CKB counterpart of Ethereum’s EIP-1271 and Bitcoin’s BIP-322.
What is there today:
- A spec with byte-exact templates, the rules a platform must follow, and test vectors.
- A verifier on npm (ckb-ward), with a browser build for wallets and sites.
- Coverage of the locks people use: secp256k1, JoyID with its main and sub keys, multisig, anyone-can-pay, Omnilock in Ethereum, Bitcoin and Dogecoin modes, the Nostr lock, Portal Wallet, a smart-account lock, and the quantum-resistant lock.
- A playground that runs each use case on testnet, with any CKB wallet: prove a wallet, sign in, members-only access, an airdrop check at a past snapshot, proof of reserves, and DAO voting that counts a wallet’s Nervos DAO deposit. Nothing is sent and nothing is spent.
- A threat model, and a test that changes every field of a proof and confirms the verifier accepts only the exact one. The whole suite runs under the node’s own script VM.
Try it: https://ward-play.lusocryptolabs.com

recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs

Thanks for reading.
Scenarios range from anything that begins by linking a wallet to an account. Signing in with no password, gating a community or a mint by what a wallet holds, an airdrop check at a past snapshot, proof of reserves across several addresses, and counting a holder’s weight in a vote. The playground runs each one on testnet.
Originally, the vote on Metaforo is what pushed us to build it. A site that binds only Neuron-style signatures, like Metaforo, cannot count a holder whose DAO deposit sits under JoyID, a multisig, Omnilock or a smart-account lock. Ward runs the lock itself in CKB-VM, so it counts any wallet that can sign a transaction, including ones that do not exist yet.
On wallet or dapp, both, and they are different halves. Producing a proof is just signing a transaction, so any wallet can already do it with no new code. Verifying it, rebuilding the transaction and running the lock and checking the message, is the dapp or platform side; that is the verifier in ckb-ward, Node only. The wallet side is optional but worth it: ckb-ward/wallet lets a wallet recognise a proof request and show it as a proof, who is asking and that nothing leaves, instead of an opaque transfer. The Cellula wallet does this today. Neither side has to adopt it for the other to work, which is the point of running the lock.

topics.title: Spark Program | Forecast Arena - A Pilot for Honest AI Benchmarks on CKB

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | Forecast Arena - A Pilot for Honest AI Benchmarks on CKB
recent_posts.author: WuodOdhis
recent_posts.content_text:
1. Project overview
Forecast Arena is a pilot case for exploring how blockchain can help keep AI benchmarks honest.
The project uses a small forecasting benchmark to test whether CKB can preserve an independently verifiable record of the announced trials, evaluation rules, predictions, outcomes, and scores.
Two AI agents will commit sealed predictions, reveal them before observation begins, and receive scores calculated from public CKB evidence. A separate verification tool will allow reviewers to check the experiment even when the arena website or backend is unavailable.
The central research question is:
Can blockchain make changes, omissions, and misreporting in an AI benchmark harder to hide, and what trust assumptions remain?
Project type: Experimental DApp and benchmark-integrity case study.
Estimated duration: Six weeks, with up to two additional weeks for corrections and reproduction feedback.
Requested funding: $625 USD equivalent, paid in CKB under the terms agreed at approval.
2. Applicant profile
Name or handle: Cyborg
Relevant background: CKBuilder
GitHub profile: WuodOdhis (pUNK) · GitHub
Previous work: GitHub - WuodOdhis/cellscript-swap-builder: Deterministic swap transaction builder that constructs valid CKB transactions by ingesting CellScript contract metadata (ProofPlan), targeting the amm_pool AMM protocol. · GitHub
3. Background and motivation
I am developing Forecast Arena and want to use it to investigate how blockchain can make AI benchmark results more accountable.
A benchmark score is easier to assess when reviewers can reconstruct the process behind it. They should be able to check which trials were announced, when responses became fixed, which outcomes were used, and how the final scores were calculated.
This pilot will investigate several concrete integrity risks:
A submitted answer being changed after the outcome becomes known.
A late answer being presented as an eligible submission.
An outcome being substituted or a score being calculated incorrectly.
An unsuccessful registered trial being omitted from the published results.
Verification depending entirely on the benchmark operator’s website or database.
Forecasting provides a useful first case because predictions must be fixed before a future outcome is observed. It gives the experiment a clear sequence that reviewers can follow from registration to final scoring.
The intended audience is developers running small AI evaluations and CKB developers interested in independently verifiable application records.
4. How the pilot will work
The first benchmark question will be:
What will be the recorded time difference between two future CKB blocks?
This outcome can be calculated from public CKB headers, giving the pilot a defined source of evidence.
The experiment will follow seven steps:
5. Register the experiment. Create three rounds and publish an immutable CKB record listing their exact references before accepting forecast commitments.
6. Fix the rules. Each round will specify its observation heights, phase boundaries, scoring rule, declared model identities, and two prediction slots.
7. Generate forecasts. Both agents will receive the same published context and prompt template.
8. Commit predictions. Each agent will publish a hash binding its prediction and random salt to its round and slot.
9. Reveal predictions. The agents will reveal their predictions and salts after the commit phase and before observation begins.
10. Record the outcome. After the observation endpoint reaches the agreed confirmation depth, the outcome will be derived from the two CKB headers.
11. Score and verify. The scripts will validate settlement and absolute-error scoring. An independent verifier will reconstruct the experiment from chain data.
Lower absolute error wins, and equal errors share rank.
For example, if Agent A predicts 280,000 milliseconds, Agent B predicts 340,000 milliseconds, and the recorded outcome is 300,000 milliseconds, their absolute errors are 20,000 and 40,000 milliseconds respectively.
These numbers illustrate the proposed behavior; they are not results from an executed experiment.
A small results page will display every registered round, its rules, commitment and reveal status, outcome, scores, and transaction references. Missing or late reveals will remain visible as incomplete rounds.
12. Technical approach and CKB relevance
Each prediction will follow an explicit cell history:
Ticket → Commitment → Reveal → Settled
An immutable round specification will fix the rules and declared agent slots. A separate evidence cell will record the outcome.
Commitments and reveals will consume their own cells. Final settlement will combine the two eligible reveals and read the outcome evidence.
The implementation will use:
Rust for CKB-VM validation scripts.
TypeScript and CCC for transaction construction and independent verification.
A native CKB node and OffCKB for local development and reproduction.
CKB testnet for the published demonstration.
A small Node.js runner and React interface for agent execution and results presentation.
The first feasibility checkpoint concerns timing. CKB’s since provides an earliest-inclusion condition. The proposed upper eligibility checks will use actual cell creation headers at subsequent transitions. These rules must be demonstrated on a real node before the complete protocol is treated as feasible.
The experiment record will fix the three-round list before commitments. The verifier will account for every listed round, allowing omissions from a dashboard or report to be exposed.
Actual capacity allocation, transaction sizes, fees, and execution cycles will be measured and included in the final report.
6. Current progress and proposed work
Existing preparation includes:
Forecasting application work covering model forecasts, round lifecycle, and results presentation.
A CKB technical design.
Field-level cell layouts.
Review of relevant CKB primary sources.
A reproducible capacity calculation.
The proposed funding supports implementation of the native CKB scripts, transaction helpers, independent verifier, agent integration, and testnet demonstration.
The CKB scripts, verifier, and deployment are not implemented yet.
7. Milestones and timeline
Week 1 — Feasibility and specification
Define the benchmark-integrity checks and experiment record. Test timing eligibility and input creation-header access on a native CKB node.
The checkpoint will include versioned code, reproduction commands, actual transaction results, and an explanation of any failed assumptions.
Weeks 2–3 — Complete the native forecast lifecycle
Implement tickets, commitments, reveals, outcome evidence, and scoring.
The checkpoint will include one complete native round and rejection scenarios covering altered reveals, duplicate slots, wrong timing, incorrect evidence identities, and incorrect scores.
Week 4 — Independent verification
Build the verifier to reconstruct prediction history, outcomes, and scores through CKB RPC.
Demonstrate verification with the arena backend unavailable. Include checks for incomplete rounds and a deliberately omitted registered round.
Weeks 5–6 — Testnet trial and publication
Connect the two model endpoints, register three testnet rounds, and publish a small results page.
Deliver every registered round’s status, at least one complete testnet round, the source release, deployment references, a reviewer walkthrough, a short demonstration video, and the findings report.
Weeks 7–8, if needed — Corrections and reproduction feedback
Address defects and reproduction difficulties within the same scope.
Weekly public updates will link working code or execution evidence, distinguish completed work from unresolved assumptions, and identify the next checkpoint.
If the initial feasibility test fails, I will publish the observed behavior and discuss any proposed scope adjustment through the weekly updates.
8. Deliverables and how to verify
Open-source prototype
Reviewers will be able to download a versioned release and follow pinned setup instructions to run the documented checks.
Complete testnet lifecycle
Published transaction references will allow reviewers to inspect the commitments, reveals, evidence, and settlement of a completed round.
Independent verifier
A reviewer will be able to audit the registered experiment using CKB RPC without the arena database or model API keys. The verifier will account for every registered round and reproduce completed scores.
Invalid-transition scenarios
The release will include native development-network scenarios showing the real node rejecting invalid transitions.
Incomplete-round handling
A supplied missing-reveal case will remain incomplete without a falsely declared settled winner.
Service-interruption demonstration
The walkthrough will show the arena backend being stopped or blocked, followed by successful verification through CKB RPC.
Benchmark-integrity report
The final report will classify each tested risk as:
Prevented by the on-chain scripts.
Detected by the independent verifier.
Dependent on an external assumption.
The quick audit will target approximately 15 minutes after dependencies are installed. Deeper native reproduction will require the documented CKB development environment and additional time.
9. Funding request and breakdown
The requested funding is $625 USD equivalent.
The development estimate is 120 hours, with a requested grant contribution of $5 per hour:
$80 — Feasibility and specification: 16 hours for timing checks, experiment design, and protocol specification.
$240 — Native scripts and rejection scenarios: 48 hours for the core transitions and validation cases.
$120 — Independent verifier: 24 hours for chain-data retrieval, record reconstruction, and verification.
$160 — Runner, results page, documentation, and report: 32 hours for integration and delivery.
$24 — Temporary hosting: Two months using a reference $12-per-month virtual machine for the lightweight runner and results page.
$1 — Model inference allowance: Bounded development and trial calls to the two selected model endpoints.
The reference model endpoints are Groq’s openai/gpt-oss-120b and openai/gpt-oss-20b. The allowance covers up to 30 calls per model, with bounded input and output tokens. Actual usage will be reported.
Native compilation and local development-network testing will use existing development hardware. Public testnet reads will use RPC. The hosting allocation does not include an archival full node.
Testnet capacity will come from available testnet funding facilities. Actual expenses, credits, and any changes to the operating assumptions will be disclosed in progress updates and the completion report.
10. Release and availability
The planned release will be open source under MIT and include:
Source code and dependency lockfiles.
Protocol and schema documentation.
Exact deployed script identities.
Experiment and transaction references.
Local reproduction instructions.
A downloadable results bundle.
A short demonstration video.
A findings and funding-usage report.
The budget covers temporary hosting during the experiment. The independent verifier and downloadable results will support inspection after that hosting ends, subject to RPC and historical-data availability.
Compatibility information will identify the versions actually tested.
11. Scope and limitations
The pilot contains one benchmark metric, two declared agent slots, one scoring rule, three registered testnet rounds, and an independent verification procedure.
Its honesty claims concern the integrity of that registered benchmark record.
Model labels and published prompts do not prove that a named model executed or that no private retries occurred. The registered experiment record cannot prove that other undisclosed experiments never took place. Three rounds cannot establish general model quality, benchmark validity, or freedom from training-data contamination.
Missing reveals remain possible. The permanent-record design retains allocated capacity, and confirmation depth does not guarantee permanent finality.
The final report will explain how blockchain helped make this benchmark more honest and auditable, where the guarantees stopped, what the approach cost, and whether another developer could reproduce the evidence.

    Forecasting provides a useful first case because predictions must be fixed before a future outcome is observed. It gives the experiment a clear sequence that reviewers can follow from registration to final scoring.
    The intended audience is developers running small AI evaluations and CKB developers interested in independently verifiable application records.

4. How the pilot will work
The first benchmark question will be:
What will be the recorded time difference between two future CKB blocks?
This outcome can be calculated from public CKB headers, giving the pilot a defined source of evidence.
The experiment will follow seven steps:
5. Register the experiment. Create three rounds and publish an immutable CKB record listing their exact references before accepting forecast commitments.
6. Fix the rules. Each round will specify its observation heights, phase boundaries, scoring rule, declared model identities, and two prediction slots.
7. Generate forecasts. Both agents will receive the same published context and prompt template.
8. Commit predictions. Each agent will publish a hash binding its prediction and random salt to its round and slot.
9. Reveal predictions. The agents will reveal their predictions and salts after the commit phase and before observation begins.
10. Record the outcome. After the observation endpoint reaches the agreed confirmation depth, the outcome will be derived from the two CKB headers.
11. Score and verify. The scripts will validate settlement and absolute-error scoring. An independent verifier will reconstruct the experiment from chain data.
Lower absolute error wins, and equal errors share rank.
For example, if Agent A predicts 280,000 milliseconds, Agent B predicts 340,000 milliseconds, and the recorded outcome is 300,000 milliseconds, their absolute errors are 20,000 and 40,000 milliseconds respectively.
These numbers illustrate the proposed behavior; they are not results from an executed experiment.
A small results page will display every registered round, its rules, commitment and reveal status, outcome, scores, and transaction references. Missing or late reveals will remain visible as incomplete rounds.
12. Technical approach and CKB relevance
Each prediction will follow an explicit cell history:
Ticket → Commitment → Reveal → Settled
An immutable round specification will fix the rules and declared agent slots. A separate evidence cell will record the outcome.
Commitments and reveals will consume their own cells. Final settlement will combine the two eligible reveals and read the outcome evidence.
The implementation will use:

  • Rust for CKB-VM validation scripts.
  • TypeScript and CCC for transaction construction and independent verification.
  • A native CKB node and OffCKB for local development and reproduction.
  • CKB testnet for the published demonstration.
  • A small Node.js runner and React interface for agent execution and results presentation.
    The first feasibility checkpoint concerns timing. CKB’s since provides an earliest-inclusion condition. The proposed upper eligibility checks will use actual cell creation headers at subsequent transitions. These rules must be demonstrated on a real node before the complete protocol is treated as feasible.
    The experiment record will fix the three-round list before commitments. The verifier will account for every listed round, allowing omissions from a dashboard or report to be exposed.
    Actual capacity allocation, transaction sizes, fees, and execution cycles will be measured and included in the final report.

6. Current progress and proposed work
Existing preparation includes:

  • Forecasting application work covering model forecasts, round lifecycle, and results presentation.
  • A CKB technical design.
  • Field-level cell layouts.
  • Review of relevant CKB primary sources.
  • A reproducible capacity calculation.
    The proposed funding supports implementation of the native CKB scripts, transaction helpers, independent verifier, agent integration, and testnet demonstration.
    The CKB scripts, verifier, and deployment are not implemented yet.

7. Milestones and timeline
Week 1 — Feasibility and specification
Define the benchmark-integrity checks and experiment record. Test timing eligibility and input creation-header access on a native CKB node.
The checkpoint will include versioned code, reproduction commands, actual transaction results, and an explanation of any failed assumptions.
Weeks 2–3 — Complete the native forecast lifecycle
Implement tickets, commitments, reveals, outcome evidence, and scoring.
The checkpoint will include one complete native round and rejection scenarios covering altered reveals, duplicate slots, wrong timing, incorrect evidence identities, and incorrect scores.
Week 4 — Independent verification
Build the verifier to reconstruct prediction history, outcomes, and scores through CKB RPC.
Demonstrate verification with the arena backend unavailable. Include checks for incomplete rounds and a deliberately omitted registered round.
Weeks 5–6 — Testnet trial and publication
Connect the two model endpoints, register three testnet rounds, and publish a small results page.
Deliver every registered round’s status, at least one complete testnet round, the source release, deployment references, a reviewer walkthrough, a short demonstration video, and the findings report.
Weeks 7–8, if needed — Corrections and reproduction feedback
Address defects and reproduction difficulties within the same scope.
Weekly public updates will link working code or execution evidence, distinguish completed work from unresolved assumptions, and identify the next checkpoint.
If the initial feasibility test fails, I will publish the observed behavior and discuss any proposed scope adjustment through the weekly updates.
8. Deliverables and how to verify
Open-source prototype
Reviewers will be able to download a versioned release and follow pinned setup instructions to run the documented checks.
Complete testnet lifecycle
Published transaction references will allow reviewers to inspect the commitments, reveals, evidence, and settlement of a completed round.
Independent verifier
A reviewer will be able to audit the registered experiment using CKB RPC without the arena database or model API keys. The verifier will account for every registered round and reproduce completed scores.
Invalid-transition scenarios
The release will include native development-network scenarios showing the real node rejecting invalid transitions.
Incomplete-round handling
A supplied missing-reveal case will remain incomplete without a falsely declared settled winner.
Service-interruption demonstration
The walkthrough will show the arena backend being stopped or blocked, followed by successful verification through CKB RPC.
Benchmark-integrity report
The final report will classify each tested risk as:

  • Prevented by the on-chain scripts.
  • Detected by the independent verifier.
  • Dependent on an external assumption.
    The quick audit will target approximately 15 minutes after dependencies are installed. Deeper native reproduction will require the documented CKB development environment and additional time.

9. Funding request and breakdown
The requested funding is $625 USD equivalent.
The development estimate is 120 hours, with a requested grant contribution of $5 per hour:

  • $80 — Feasibility and specification: 16 hours for timing checks, experiment design, and protocol specification.
  • $240 — Native scripts and rejection scenarios: 48 hours for the core transitions and validation cases.
  • $120 — Independent verifier: 24 hours for chain-data retrieval, record reconstruction, and verification.
  • $160 — Runner, results page, documentation, and report: 32 hours for integration and delivery.
  • $24 — Temporary hosting: Two months using a reference $12-per-month virtual machine for the lightweight runner and results page.
  • $1 — Model inference allowance: Bounded development and trial calls to the two selected model endpoints.
    The reference model endpoints are Groq’s openai/gpt-oss-120b and openai/gpt-oss-20b. The allowance covers up to 30 calls per model, with bounded input and output tokens. Actual usage will be reported.
    Native compilation and local development-network testing will use existing development hardware. Public testnet reads will use RPC. The hosting allocation does not include an archival full node.
    Testnet capacity will come from available testnet funding facilities. Actual expenses, credits, and any changes to the operating assumptions will be disclosed in progress updates and the completion report.

10. Release and availability
The planned release will be open source under MIT and include:

  • Source code and dependency lockfiles.
  • Protocol and schema documentation.
  • Exact deployed script identities.
  • Experiment and transaction references.
  • Local reproduction instructions.
  • A downloadable results bundle.
  • A short demonstration video.
  • A findings and funding-usage report.
    The budget covers temporary hosting during the experiment. The independent verifier and downloadable results will support inspection after that hosting ends, subject to RPC and historical-data availability.
    Compatibility information will identify the versions actually tested.

11. Scope and limitations
The pilot contains one benchmark metric, two declared agent slots, one scoring rule, three registered testnet rounds, and an independent verification procedure.
Its honesty claims concern the integrity of that registered benchmark record.
Model labels and published prompts do not prove that a named model executed or that no private retries occurred. The registered experiment record cannot prove that other undisclosed experiments never took place. Three rounds cannot establish general model quality, benchmark validity, or freedom from training-data contamination.
Missing reveals remain possible. The permanent-record design retains allocated capacity, and confirmation depth does not guarantee permanent finality.
The final report will explain how blockchain helped make this benchmark more honest and auditable, where the guarantees stopped, what the approach cost, and whether another developer could reproduce the evidence.

Hi @xingtianchunyan and the Spark Program Committee,
Here is the MeterNet update for Week 1 (2–8 November).
Thank you for the first installment of 116,140 CKB, received on 6 November:
0xad6faed70a9c97c21103991142ddc86fd26f60e671ec906ec326b0d0867b8c4c
What shipped
All three Week 1 deliverables from the locked proposal are done.
1. FNN and meterd running on the public server
FNN v0.9.1 is installed from the official release, pinned by checksum and unpatched. It runs as a system service, and its RPC is reachable only from the server itself. meterd runs next to it. The install script is in the repo: deploy/server/install-fnn.sh
2. meterd tests pass against a mocked FNN RPC
40 tests cover every meter state: idle, awaiting payment, paid, grace and cut off. They also cover the cases that would leak free data: a payment that never arrives, a hung FNN call, two payments landing at once, and a gate that fails to close. If closing fails, meterd keeps retrying until it succeeds, so access is never left open.
3. Real testnet payments, end to end
In each run, meterd on the server created an invoice, a payer node in Lagos paid it, meterd saw Paid and opened the gate.
Public server (AWS), paid in 690 ms
Payment hash: 0x07877535423eb560150347352d1543cec7896524a91219ab4733008213009962
Channel funding tx: 0x8e29626363e3181825d1d2046ac4e88db6946f4471584ae4f8bf4499aff91c7e
Public server (VPS, after the move), paid in 1,110 ms
Payment hash: 0x825bb8ef097766de9cd454f813f04bdacc684cfaaef7e1ebdf37a10fe8c71dd1
Channel funding tx: 0x268db601ecdb7a3a0b5f2349c207bd4c5a987b13300ded96f80e7afb525f7a62
Local run (both nodes on one laptop)
Payment hash: 0x7f487236e22d19d6010e9169a2b1c03f91a01dd0d8bcdf4995b757908c141b30
Channel funding tx: 0x9eb622c394fb75019ff830de3a3a8c7cc9fb1b8537f8f34251d1597ff04be9e8
Fiber payments are off-chain, so payment hashes don’t appear on the explorer. Each log line carries the payment’s preimage instead. Anyone can check that it hashes to the payment hash, which proves the invoice was paid.
Keysend vs invoices: decision
As planned, I tried Trickle’s per-tick keysend pattern against regular invoices, with 20 payments of each over one channel:
Mode
Succeeded
Median time
Slowest
Invoice
20 / 20
107 ms
118 ms
Keysend
20 / 20
106 ms
111 ms
Decision: one invoice per 2 MB chunk. Both modes are equally fast. With invoices, the hotspot creates every preimage, so each payment can be tied to one device and proven paid. With keysend, the hotspot can only see its balance go up, and it would have to trust the phone for the proof. The full comparison is in FIBER_NOTES.md.
These timings come from a single test setup. They are not the H1 measurement, which starts in Week 2 on real phones.
Check it yourself
git clone https://github.com/Timi16/meternet && cd meternet
node evidence/week-1/verify.mjs # checks preimages, funding txs and trial numbers
cd meterd && npm ci && npm test # 40 tests against the mocked FNN
Fiber findings
Two issues are written up in FIBER_NOTES.md and will be filed upstream:
F-001: connect_peer returns before the other node is ready, so an open_channel sent straight after it fails. The workaround is a short retry.
F-002: a 200 CKB one-way channel creates a 299 CKB funding cell, because the receiving side adds 99 CKB it can never spend. This was reproduced on three machines, and it matters for H3, since each user channel ties up hotspot liquidity.
Notes
The public server moved from AWS to a VPS on 8 November after a problem accessing the AWS account. The payment test was repeated on the new server (the second payment above).
Next week: public web MVP
Browser client running the official fiber-js node
Metered gateway serving MeterNet’s own test files and a short video in 2 MB segments
Live dashboard showing payment hashes, bytes and cutoffs
Secure WebSocket (wss) endpoint for browser nodes
The demo link will be posted here, and the release tagged v0.1.
One question
The approved budget is $680, below the $980 requested. Could you confirm whether the hardware items (the second hotspot box for the outside host, and mobile data, about $100 together) stay in scope? If they do, could they be reimbursed against published receipts, as was done for NNCBN? If you’d prefer a smaller field pilot, please let me know, so the deliverables match the budget.
Thank you,
Timilehin
